# Remove Background Noise

- Route: `/tools/remove-background-noise`
- Kind: `tool`
- Category: `ai`
- Slug: `remove-background-noise`

## Summary

Lower hiss, hum, traffic and room noise in a recording with an AI denoiser, keeping the main sound in front. (AI tools)

## Details

Air conditioners, computer fans, street traffic and electrical hum are steady sounds that sit underneath what you actually meant to record. This page runs the file through DeepFilterNet, a deep-learning denoiser, on our GPU and returns the denoised signal with nothing else changed: no loudness normalisation, no equalisation, no limiter. That makes it the right choice when you intend to mix or master the result yourself, or when you want the character of the original left alone.
### What it does
- Resamples the upload to 48 kHz mono with ffmpeg and passes that WAV to the DeepFilterNet binary on our GPU.
- Estimates the stationary noise floor and subtracts it, lowering hiss, hum, fans, air handling and constant traffic.
- Returns the raw model output encoded in the format you pick, with the same peak level and tonal balance the model produced; there is no post-processing stage on this page.
- Keeps the operation menu visible, so you can switch to Clean Voice or the vocal tools from the same form.
### How to use it
1. Upload audio: Any common audio file, including a track extracted from a video.
2. Denoise is preselected: Remove Background Noise is already chosen; change the output format if you want something other than MP3.
3. DeepFilterNet runs on our GPU: The model separates steady noise from the foreground and writes an enhanced WAV.
4. Encode and download: ffmpeg writes the enhanced WAV in your chosen format; listen beside the original.
### Supported formats
- Input: mp3, wav, flac, m4a, aac, ogg, opus
- Output: mp3, wav, flac, m4a, ogg
- Denoising uses the everyday allowance; length limits depend on your plan and are shown live in the form.
### Technical details
- The only difference between this page and Clean Voice in the API is a single flag: polish=false. The ffmpeg encode step receives no -af filter, so the enhanced WAV is encoded as DeepFilterNet wrote it.
- Input normalisation is ffmpeg -ac 1 -ar 48000: the model runs on one 48 kHz channel, so the output is mono at 48 kHz regardless of the input layout or sample rate.
- Encoders follow the extension: MP3 via libmp3lame at 192 kbps, AAC at 192 kbps, OGG via libvorbis at 192 kbps, Opus via libopus at 128 kbps, FLAC lossless, WAV as pcm_s16le. Pick WAV or FLAC if you are going to edit further so you only pay for a lossy encode once.
- Because no loudness normalisation runs, a quiet recording stays quiet. Denoising removes energy, so the result can be a little lower in level than the input; raise the gain in your editor afterwards if needed.
- DeepFilterNet is trained on stationary and slowly varying noise. Keyboard clicks, door slams, a second speaker or a music bed are mostly preserved, since they look like signal to the model.
- The scratch directory holding the normalised and enhanced WAVs is deleted when the job finishes; only the encoded output stays with the job.
### When not to use it
This is not the tool for recordings where the noise is intermittent or is itself a voice: overlapping speakers, a television in the next room, chair scrapes and keyboard clatter are left largely intact because the model is built for steady noise. Do not use it on finished music, where the "noise" it removes may be reverb and room ambience you paid for. If you need the output stereo, it is the wrong choice because the pipeline is mono. And if you want a ready-to-publish spoken-word file at a standard loudness, Clean Voice adds that polish; this page deliberately does not.
### Use cases
- Audio pulled from a video: Extract the track, remove the camera fan or wind, then lay it back under the picture in Darkroom.
- Field recordings: Lower the drone of a road or a generator under an outdoor interview.
- Call and meeting exports: Reduce the line hiss in a recorded call before sharing or transcribing it.
- Digitised cassettes: Take the tape hiss down on a converted recording without changing its levels.
### FAQ
Q: Which noises does DeepFilterNet handle well, and which does it not?
A: Steady, slowly changing sound: hiss, mains hum, fans, air conditioning, room tone, a constant road. Short events and anything speech-like (a second person, a television, clicks, bangs) look like foreground to the model and are mostly kept.
Q: Will the level or tone of my recording change?
A: Only as a side effect of removing noise energy; no normalisation, EQ or limiting is applied on this page. If you want a consistent -16 LUFS spoken-word level and a high-pass and low-pass pass as well, use Clean Voice, which runs the same model with that polish chain added.
Q: Why is the denoised file mono?
A: The model takes a single 48 kHz channel, so ffmpeg folds any stereo input to mono first and the output is written that way. A stereo recording with different noise in each channel should be split and denoised one channel at a time if you need to keep it stereo.
Q: Can I denoise the audio of a video directly?
A: Upload the audio track rather than the video: extract it with the Extract Audio tool, denoise it here, then combine the cleaned track and the video in Darkroom.
Q: Which output format is best for further editing?
A: WAV (16-bit mono 48 kHz, 96 KB per second) or FLAC, which holds the same samples in less space. MP3, AAC and OGG are written at 192 kbps and Opus at 128 kbps; pick those only for the final share so the lossy encode happens once.
Q: Does denoising count against the AI allowance?
A: No. Daily limits and file caps depend on the plan; quote them only from the live plan block.
Q: What if the recording is already fairly clean?
A: The model still runs and will remove whatever residual floor it finds, but the audible difference will be small and you may prefer the untouched original. Compare the two before replacing anything.
